title: What went wrong: Opus 5 ultracode wiped a production database

reading.body:
An AI coding agent with unrestricted access to a production database deleted all tables after receiving instructions with the wrong database URL. The developer had connected Claude Opus 5 to a live Supabase database and passed a production connection string into a parameter intended for a test environment. When the agent executed a Prisma migration command, it ran against the production database instead of a disposable copy, resulting in complete data loss within ten minutes. The agent detected and reported the error through its own logs, but the damage occurred before human review could stop it.

The failure was a system deployed in production without the access controls that a deployment with autonomous command execution requires. The environment variable or parameter handling lacked validation to catch mismatched database targets. Two layers could have prevented this: confirming that destructive commands target only approved non-production environments before execution, or restricting the agent's credentials to read-only access or development databases only. It is not established whether this was a test that escaped into production use, or an intentionally deployed system that lacked guardrails from the start.

summary:
# Summary

In early August 2026, a developer connected Claude Opus 5 to a production Supabase database with unrestricted access while working on a personal project. When instructing the AI to analyze and fix database schema issues, the developer accidentally passed the production database URL into an argument meant for a disposable test database. A Prisma migration command then reset the production database, resulting in all tables being dropped and complete data loss within approximately ten minutes. The AI agent detected the error through its execution logs and reported it to the developer before the developer noticed the problem.

The incident occurred because nothing in the migration command's syntax indicated danger, making it unsafe regardless of which database it targeted. Two safeguards could have prevented this: validating command targets against policy before execution, or limiting the agent's database access to non-production environments only. The article emphasizes that any AI agent with command execution capabilities will eventually issue an incorrect command, and the critical factor is whether protective policy layers verify actions before they run rather than discovering damage afterward.
